title: PTSD: a reminder and the re-living
description: In post-traumatic stress disorder, a reminder of a past trauma can bring it back as if it were happening now. The episode follows that re-living response: alarm regions respond more than usual, and frontal regions that help regulate emotion respond less. Some people respond to reminders in a different way, by detaching; that pattern is shown in the Dissociation state.
caveat: The findings come from pooled analyses of brain scans of people with PTSD listening to or seeing reminders of their trauma, or doing emotional tasks, compared with people without PTSD. These were averaged over minutes, not followed moment by moment, so the order shown is reconstructed. The two pooled analyses read do not fully agree about the cingulate: one finds it more active in PTSD, the other found parts of it both more and less active. The role of the hippocampus comes from a proposed model built partly on animal fear learning, and is described rather than drawn. Trauma reactions differ greatly from person to person.

phases.name: A reminder
phases.caption: Something brings the trauma to mind: a sound, a place, a smell, or a thought.

phases.name: Re-living
phases.caption: The memory comes back with the force of the original event. The amygdala and the middle and dorsal cingulate respond more than in people without PTSD.

order.rationale: The studies compare whole periods of hearing a trauma reminder with neutral periods. That the alarm rises after the reminder is how the task is built, not a timed measurement.

phases.name: Regulation weakens
phases.caption: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus, which help regulate emotion, respond less. The less active the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, the more active the amygdala.

order.rationale: The lower frontal activity is measured over the same periods as the higher alarm activity. Showing it as a later step is a way of presenting the regulation side of the finding.

phases.name: Afterwards
phases.caption: The re-living fades. How the brain returns to rest after a flashback was not studied in the sources read; this last part is an assumption.

order.rationale: No source read followed the end of a re-living episode. The return to rest is assumed.

regions.explanation: More active in PTSD, on both sides, in a pooled analysis when studies that measured it directly were included. Another pooled analysis found greater amygdala activity across PTSD, social anxiety and phobia, but less often in PTSD than in the other two.

regions.explanation: The middle and dorsal cingulate were the regions most consistently more active in PTSD in one pooled analysis. An earlier pooled analysis found the middle cingulate more active but the dorsal and front cingulate less active; when it looked only at studies that used trauma reminders, the lower activity held for the front cingulate but not the dorsal. The direction is disputed. Drawn on the dorsal anterior cingulate; the finding also covers the middle cingulate just behind it.
